newsitem.title: UK: Funds show new interest in UK manufacturers.
newsitem.headline: Funds show new interest in UK manufacturers.

text.p: Cheered by sterling's retreat and the diminished threat of large interest rate rises, fund managers said they are showing renewed interest in hard-hit British manufacturing shares.

The sector has, until recently, been deeply unfashionable, as sterling's ascent cast a pall over companies with overseas earnings. But with dizzying valuations in other sectors and markets, fund managers are taking a long look at industrial companies.

"There has been an almost indiscriminate hit across the market," said Mark Crutchley, who as head of UK balanced funds at Gartmore Investment Management looks after 1.25 billion sterling in UK shares.
"The manufacturing sector has been severely hit by currency moves and a lot of shares had gone down by more than was warranted."

Sterling's ease from an eight-year high of 3.0878 marks on July 23 to around 2.95 on Tuesday has taken some of the heat off exporters, fund managers say, and led to a brisk rally in mid- and small-capitalisation industrial shares.

Since that sterling peak, the manufacturing-oriented FTSE 250 has risen more than four percent, but is still up just over five percent on the year. That compares with the blue chip FTSE 100's 24 percent rise.
"We would expect to see the bounce continue. I think there are still quite a few stocks that we would be quite interested in buying," Crutchley said.
"The UK economy is running along pretty strongly and a lot of companies that are UK-orientated and have had very good domestic order books have been dragged down along with the exporters."

Sandy Nairn, global equity strategist at Templeton Investment Management in Edinburgh, has been moving funds in his global equity portfolio into UK manufacturers. He still sees some bargains out there.
"There has been a gut reaction against UK manufacturers," he said.

"UK industry, like U.S. industry, has substantially restructured. For exporters, sterling strength is a concern and that will hit margins," he said. "But their ability to continue to produce reasonable profits in the long term is undiminished."
He added the impact of the dramatic rise in the pound had now been largely discounted.

While the British economy is buoyant, there has some speculation among economists the Bank of England's programme of tightenings could lead to a hard landing, a threat which has also weighed on manufacturers' shares.
But that fear too may be receding, they said.
"If you take the Bank of England Monetary Committee to have said that interest rates are not going much higher, then manufacturers are not looking at a downturn," Crutchley said.
Crutchley's balanced pension funds are overweight manufacturers by between 10 to 20 percent relative to the market weighting.
To be sure, investment managers are not unanimous in re-rating the sector.
Roger Cursley, who manages 800 million sterling of UK smaller companies shares for Fleming Investment Management, thinks there is still a lot of pain from sterling strength to be recognised.
"I still don't think, looking at the smaller end of the market, analysts' forecasts are yet to take account of sterling at 2.90 to the mark -- let alone 3.0."
"I think we are going to have a rough result season."
Vanessa James, head of UK equities at Legal & General Investment Management, agrees that sterling at this level will hamper earnings growth.
"I would not chase some of these prices now in the manufacturing area."
"The call at some point is going to be to go out of the financials, the pharmaceuticals, and the oils and go into general industrials. I just think it is too soon to do that."
